question: Na slovenskej svadbe DJ okolo polnoci stíši tanečnú hudbu, lebo prichádza starý obrad: neveste zložia závoj a namiesto neho jej nasadia niečo iné. Čo?
source_excerpt: Married women take down the hair chaplet of the bride and put on a bonnet instead.

extra.why_interesting: Players have all seen the music stop at midnight at a Slovak wedding, but may never have put a name on what the veil gets swapped for and why. The answer clicks instantly: of course, that is the whole point of the ritual.
extra.verification_notes: Midnight čepčenie, where the bride's wreath or veil is replaced by a čepiec (bonnet), is the standard Slovak custom; a scarf variant exists but čepiec remains the canonical answer (https://spectator.sme.sk/culture-and-lifestyle/c/kidnapping-and-virginity-brace-yourself-for-a-slovak-wedding).

explanation: Čepiec bol znakom vydatej ženy. Odtiaľ pochádza aj slovo čepčenie a hovorí sa, že nevesta je odvtedy „pod čepcom“.

question: Slávny Mendelssohnov Svadobný pochod, ktorý pustí takmer každý svadobný DJ, nevznikol pre kostol, ale ako hudba k divadelnej hre od Shakespeara. Ku ktorej?
source_excerpt: comes from Felix Mendelssohn's incidental music for Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the tune from weddings and assumes it was written for a church ceremony. It actually comes from theatre music for a comedy full of fairies and love potions. Players can reason toward it: it is a Shakespeare play that ends in weddings, so it must be a comedy.
extra.verification_notes: The Wedding March is from Mendelssohn's incidental music (Op. 61) for Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream (Sen noci svätojánskej), per Wikipedia.

explanation: Je to komédia o vílach a čarovnom nápoji lásky, v ktorej sa kráľovná víl zaľúbi do muža s oslou hlavou. Pochod v nej sprevádza trojitú svadbu na konci hry.
